title: Cheapest cables to join four towns
hook: Should you always lay the cheapest cable first? Try it on four towns.

knows: a loop: a path that comes back to where it started
doesNotKnow: that for connecting a network, taking the cheapest cable that closes no loop provably gives the cheapest network

misconception: Since greedy failed on coins, it cannot be trusted to build the cheapest network.
objective: The learner can lay AB 1, CD 1, BC 2 (total 4) by taking the cheapest cable that closes no loop, and explain why no network joining the four towns can cost less.

claims.text: With cables AB 1, BC 2, AC 2, CD 3, BD 4 and AD 5, the lowest total cost that connects all four towns is 6 (AB, BC, CD).
claims.source: Brute force over every 3-cable set in Demo.tsx (bruteMin), and Kruskal by hand: AB 1, BC 2, CD 3. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 12): node brute force over all 20 three-cable sets: min 6, achieved by AB+BC+CD and also AB+AC+CD (BC and AC tie at 2). The value 6 is right; '(AB, BC, CD)' is one of two cheapest networks.

claims.text: AC would close a loop with AB and BC, so it is refused mid-build; once AB, BC and CD are laid, BD and AD would also each close a loop.
claims.source: Demo.tsx joined(): AC joins A and C, already connected through B. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 12): True in list order (BC listed and tapped before AC): AC then joins A and C already joined via B; with AB, BC, CD laid, B-D and A-D are joined, so BD and AD close loops. Note: the stage accepts a tap on AC before BC (same cost, check is cost > cheapest), and then BC is the one refused; the stage text is dynamic and stays correct either way.

claims.text: Joining four towns takes 3 cables. The three cheapest here cost 1 + 2 + 2 = 5, but they form a loop of A, B and C and leave D out, so 5 cannot join everyone; the cheapest network that does costs 6.
claims.source: Arithmetic on the cable list; bruteMin in Demo.tsx. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 12): Spanning tree on 4 towns has 3 edges; three cheapest AB 1, BC 2, AC 2 = 5 form triangle A-B-C, D isolated; node min over connected sets = 6.

claims.text: Cheapest first, skipping cables that close a loop, always gives the cheapest network (Kruskal's algorithm).
claims.source: J. B. Kruskal, 'On the shortest spanning subtree of a graph and the traveling salesman problem', Proc. AMS 7(1), 1956; CLRS (3rd ed.) 23.2 with Corollary 23.2.

claims.text: A skipped loop never blocks a better choice later.
claims.source: Cut property / exchange argument (CLRS 23.1, Theorem 23.1): the cheapest cable across any cut is in some cheapest network, so a greedy choice can always be extended to an optimum. A refused cable joins already-joined towns, so it can never be needed. Contrast: coins 1, 5, 6 making 10 (coin-greedy-trap: greedy 6+1+1+1+1 vs 5+5). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 12): A refused cable joins towns already joined, so dropping it never changes which towns are connected; Kruskal optimality by the cut property (CLRS 3rd ed. 23.1, Thm 23.1; not opened). Housekeeping: Demo.tsx header comment still lists old costs (CD 1, min 4); not learner-facing.

recall.question: Three towns: XY costs 2, YZ costs 3, XZ costs 4. Cheapest cable first, skipping loops. What is the total?
recall.why: Take XY 2, then YZ 3: all joined for 5. XZ would close a loop and is skipped. Three towns need 2 cables, and 2 + 3 are the two cheapest.
